Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'comments on family' is not impossible as a trigger, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear assault-linked context. The other triggers and memory items point to sensory/intrusive re-experiencing, whereas this item suggests a family-related theme not represented elsewhere in threat, appraisals, or memory.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies a bereavement/loss-focused coping target, but no other selected items indicate death loss or grief as a central aspect of the assault trauma. This maladaptive strategy does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on assault-related intrusive memory, dissociation, and social avoidance.

vignette: Arthur Vance was sixty-eight when he finally walked into the clinic, his palms damp against the leather strap of his satchel. Six years earlier, the assault had unfolded in the sterile corridor of a North American medical center, where he had come to sit with a family member. The attacker, a disheveled man who had stumbled out of the waiting room, struck without warning, pressing Arthur's chest against the wall. Arthur remembered the event not as a continuous flow of time but as a series of sharp photographs: the glint of a silver watch against a pale wrist, the sudden impact of a heavy shoulder, and the way his breath caught in his throat. Each time he closed his eyes now, those same moments surfaced without transition, and the terror he had felt in that corridor rushed back into his body with the same intensity, as if the years had simply folded away. Sometimes, the pieces arrived without warning-a flash of the attacker's jacket, a phantom pressure on his ribs-appearing and vanishing in the space of a heartbeat. In the months that followed, Arthur began to notice how the hospital's antiseptic scent still clung to his own clothes after routine check-ups, and how that sharp, clean smell would suddenly pull him back into that corridor. He learned to brace himself before stepping through double doors, his shoulders rising as the air grew thick with the ghost of the attack. Alcohol smelled differently than it had before; a whiff of whiskey or beer no longer suggested relaxation but stirred a quiet alarm, a reminder of the attacker's breath and the blurred edges of the struggle. He had come to believe that the world held these lingering traces, and he stopped them by carefully curating his distance. He avoided crowded hallways, preferring the quiet of his car or the corner desk in his school counseling office. When students or parents lingered too long during consultations, when their voices softened and their gazes fixed on his, Arthur felt the familiar pull of vulnerability. He would lean back in his chair, deliberately blanking out, letting his attention drift upward as if leaving his body behind. It was a practiced exhalation, a way to step sideways from the room without actually standing up. At home, his wife noticed how he kept the sofa cushion between them when they watched television, how he rose to pour water when she reached for his hand. He kept his distance alongside a quiet vigilance over proximity and scent. The habits formed gradually, layer upon layer, until his avoidance of people and his hesitation toward intimacy stood together in the rhythm of his days. He continued to work as a school counselor, but the environment itself demanded new negotiations. The school health room, with its persistent antiseptic undertow, became a place he navigated by the walls. Staff gatherings were endured with a polite distance, and he often left early, his satchel heavy with unspoken conversations. His counseling sessions remained steady, yet he kept his desk firmly between himself and those who sought him, answering questions with measured clarity while his mind hovered just above the floor. Arthur's decision to seek help did not come from a single breaking point but from the slow accumulation of these quiet withdrawals. He had begun to notice that the photographs in his mind no longer stayed separate; they stacked upon one another, and the deliberate drifting he relied upon was beginning to feel less like relief and more like erasure. He was afraid that he was losing the texture of his own life, trading it for a careful distance. What he hoped for, he said during his first visit, was not to have the memories go away but to walk through the antiseptic aisles and the crowded school corridors without bracing for impact, to let someone sit close without feeling the walls close in, and to remember the assault without the terror rising again so quickly. He carried his satchel a little straighter now, stepping forward with the same steady pace he had used for forty years, ready to meet the world without leaving it behind.
